note: Consensus recommendations from over 200 stakeholders on validation, certification and national safety reporting.
title: Toward a responsible future: recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support
journal: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

reading.body:
This paper presents consensus recommendations from more than 200 stakeholders on validation, certification, and national safety reporting for AI-enabled clinical decision support.

A 200-plus-stakeholder consensus process is a different kind of evidence than a single research study. It reflects what a broad cross-section of the field currently agrees should happen, which is useful for a governance audit even though it is not itself empirical proof that the recommended validation and certification processes reduce harm.

The paper does not report whether any health system has yet implemented the specific certification and reporting processes it recommends, only that the recommendations were agreed upon.

explain_beginner: The question, what should hospitals, developers, and regulators actually require before trusting an AI tool that gives clinical recommendations at the point of care, often called AI enabled clinical decision support. People cared because by 2023 these tools were spreading faster than any shared rulebook for testing, labeling, or monitoring them, so a mixed group of clinicians, ethicists, developers, patients, and regulators was convened by a professional informatics association and a Boston hospital's informatics division to try to build consensus on what responsible use looks like. After webinars, a two day workshop with over 200 participants, and months of consensus building, the group landed on four recommendation areas, building trustworthy systems with equity built in from the start, verifying and certifying systems with a proposed label documenting things like training data origin and known biases, monitoring safety after launch through a shared reporting system, and training clinicians on new competencies for working with these tools. What it does not settle, none of these four recommendations existed as an enforceable standard at the time of publication, they are proposals for the field to adopt, not a description of a rule already in force.
explain_business: This paper gives buyers and developers a named checklist to work through before adopting an AI decision support tool, does the vendor document training data provenance and known biases, is there a defined recertification schedule after model updates, and what training does clinical staff need before go live. Because the paper documents that regulators' current tools cannot keep pace with continuously updating models, a purchaser should not assume a past regulatory clearance still covers a system after it has been retrained, and should ask the vendor directly how model drift is monitored after deployment. Implementing the recommended user competency training and safety monitoring infrastructure is a real added operational cost beyond the software license itself, one to budget for rather than treat as optional. None of these four recommendations are legally binding yet, so acting on them now is a voluntary risk reduction step, though the direction strongly signals where future regulation is likely headed. This is most relevant right now for any organization drafting internal AI governance policy or vendor contract language for clinical decision support tools.
explain_practitioner: Method, a consensus development process rather than an empirical study, combining four webinars in August 2023, a two day multi stakeholder workshop in September 2023 with over 200 participants, and a four month iterative Delphi style consensus process among the authors. The output is four recommendation domains, trustworthy system design with embedded equity frameworks, a proposed Unique AI Identifier label documenting training data provenance, known biases, algorithm details, intended use cases, certification duration, version history, and required training, a proposed national safety event reporting clearinghouse modeled on the FDA's MedWatch adverse event program, and defined competency and training requirements for clinicians. The group explicitly modeled its reporting idea on an existing pharmacovigilance system rather than inventing a new oversight model, treating AI decision support safety events the way drug adverse events are already tracked. The authors state real limitations directly, current FDA regulatory tools lack the agility to handle continuously updating algorithms, AI systems often cannot give a consistent, plausible explanation for a given recommendation, and fairness metrics frequently conflict with each other, meaning no single measure of fair enough exists across use cases.
